params.text:
Welcome

This module introduces the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity — the reference document that underpins research integrity across European Union research frameworks. It was developed by the BriGRETE project (Bridging the Gap: Research Ethics Training and Education), co-funded by the Erasmus+ programme.

The module is self-paced. Each chapter combines a short explanation, a visual from the source presentation, and an activity that lets you check your understanding before moving on.

params.alt: Module Structure and Linear Flow diagram: an end-to-end process moving through four stages — Introduce Principles, Explore Good Practices, Real-World Case Studies, and Reflection and Self-Assessment.

params.text:
How the Module Is Organised

The module follows a linear flow in four movements:

  1. Introduce Principles — the four foundational principles of research integrity (Chapters 5–10).
  2. Explore Good Practices — eight domains of good research practice, from the research environment through to peer review (Chapters 11–19).
  3. Real-World Case Studies — each practice domain is paired with a case scenario drawn from the companion guide, so theory meets practice immediately rather than in a separate block at the end.
  4. Reflection and Self-Assessment — terminology practice, a final assessment, and a closing summary (Chapters 20–22).

Two knowledge checks (Chapters 10 and 19) let you confirm your grasp of each half before continuing.

Working Through the Material

  • Use the Table of Contents to move between chapters, or simply page forward.
  • Video segments carry English subtitles — click the CC button to switch them on.
  • Attempt each activity before revealing the answer; the feedback explains the reasoning, not just the result.
  • Aim for 80% or above on the Final Assessment in Chapter 21.

params.text:
Two Primary Audiences

This module was written for two groups whose needs overlap but are not identical.

New members need foundational training: what research integrity means, how it differs from research ethics, and what the European Code expects of institutions and individuals.

Experienced members need updates on current developments — the 2023 revision of the Code, the treatment of artificial intelligence in research, and evolving expectations around data sharing.

Early-career researchers need foundational ethics knowledge at the point where habits are formed — during doctoral training and the first postdoctoral years.

Mid- and senior-career researchers carry supervisory and institutional responsibilities, and need to stay current on responsible research practice in order to model it credibly.

params.alt: Module Purpose and Core Objectives slide: the central statement reads 'To equip participants with practical knowledge and tools for good research practices', supported by three pillars — High Quality, Applicability, and Trustworthiness.

params.text:
What the Module Aims to Do

The purpose is practical: to equip participants with usable knowledge and tools for good research practice. Three qualities anchor that aim:

  • High quality — research that is methodologically sound and rigorously conducted.
  • Applicability — guidance that transfers into everyday decisions, not abstract principles that sit unused.
  • Trustworthiness — research the scientific community, policymakers, and the public can rely on.

metadata.title: The European Code and the Integrity Equation
metadata.extraTitle: The European Code and the Integrity Equation

params.text:
Integrity and Ethics: Related, Not Identical

Research integrity is the attitude and habit of conducting research according to appropriate ethical, legal, and professional frameworks. It is a disposition — a standing commitment to doing research properly, whether or not anyone is checking.

Research ethics is the application of ethical principles to specific aspects of a research project: how the study is designed, how participants are treated, how data are handled, and how misuse of results is prevented. Ethics typically involves formal review — most visibly through a Research Ethics Committee.

The distinction matters in practice. A researcher can satisfy every ethics procedure on paper while still reporting selectively or claiming undeserved credit. Integrity is what makes the procedures meaningful.

params.alt: Defining the Integrity Equation slide: an illustrated equation showing Internal Attitude and Habit, plus External Frameworks and Standards, equals Trustworthy Research.

params.text:
The Integrity Equation

Trustworthy research is the product of two inputs working together:

Internal attitude and habit — the individual researcher's disposition and routine practice. Necessary, but on its own inconsistent: judgement varies between people, and under pressure it varies within the same person.

External frameworks and standards — codes of conduct, institutional policy, legal requirements, and disciplinary norms. These stabilise individual judgement and make expectations explicit and reviewable.

Neither input alone is sufficient. Rules without commitment produce box-ticking; commitment without rules produces well-meaning inconsistency. Trust in science is a systemic outcome of good habits operating inside sound frameworks.

params.text:
The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity

Published by ALLEA (All European Academies) and revised in 2023, the Code is the reference document for research integrity across EU research frameworks, including Horizon Europe. It is written to apply across all disciplines and all career stages.

Its architecture is straightforward: four fundamental principles, followed by Good Research Practices organised into eight domains. This module follows that same structure.

params.alt: Ascending the Cognitive Staircase diagram: five ascending steps labelled Understand principles of responsible research, Apply good research practices, Solve dilemmas in research integrity, Promote responsible practices, and Foster better environments and address barriers.

params.text:
Five Levels of Engagement

Competence in research integrity develops in stages. The staircase describes the progression from knowing the rules to changing the conditions that make following them possible.
Know what the four principles are and what each requires. This is necessary groundwork, but on its own it changes little about daily practice.
Translate principles into routine decisions: how a protocol is written, how data are stored, how authorship is agreed. Application is where integrity becomes visible in the work itself.

Real cases rarely present a clean choice between right and wrong. They involve competing goods, incomplete information, and unequal power. Solving dilemmas means reasoning through genuine tension rather than applying a rule mechanically.
Move from personal compliance to influencing others: mentoring junior colleagues, raising concerns, and making integrity a normal topic of conversation rather than an awkward one.

panels.title: 5. Foster — better environments and address barriers

params.text: The highest level addresses the structural conditions themselves — incentive systems, assessment criteria, employment precarity — that make good practice easy or hard. Many integrity failures are environmental before they are individual.

Where This Module Takes You

Chapters 5–10 build understanding. Chapters 11–19 develop application and, through the paired case studies, the capacity to solve realistic dilemmas. The closing chapters point towards promoting and fostering — the work that continues after the module ends.

params.text:
Four Principles, One Framework

The European Code organises research integrity around four principles. They are not a checklist to be completed in sequence — they operate simultaneously, and most real integrity failures involve more than one at once.

  • Reliability — ensuring the quality of research through its design, methodology, analysis, and use of resources.
  • Honesty — developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting, and communicating research transparently, fairly, fully, and without bias.
  • Respect — for colleagues, research participants, society, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and the environment.
  • Accountability — for the research from idea to publication, for its management and organisation, for training and supervision, and for its wider societal impact.

The next four chapters take each principle in turn.

params.alt: Principle 1: Reliability in Research slide. A Quality Assurance chain runs downward through four stages: Design, Methodology, Analysis, and Use of Resources. The caption reads: ensuring the quality of research across all stages of execution.

params.text:
Quality Across the Whole Chain

Reliability means ensuring the quality of research across every stage of its execution. It is often misread as being only about replication — whether the same result appears twice. Replication matters, but reliability is broader: it concerns the soundness of the entire chain that produces a result.

Is the study capable of answering the question it poses? Reliability begins with a design appropriate to the research question — adequately powered, properly controlled, and grounded in what is already known.

Are the methods appropriate, and applied consistently? Methods should be chosen for scientific merit rather than convenience or the likelihood of producing a preferred outcome, and applied the same way throughout.

Is the analysis valid and pre-specified — or, where it departs from the plan, is that departure disclosed and justified? Undisclosed analytic flexibility is one of the most common routes to unreliable findings.
Are facilities, equipment, funding, and personnel used responsibly and for their intended purpose? Resource misuse degrades research quality and wastes capacity that other work could have used.

params.text:
Five Points Where Honesty Applies

Honesty requires that research be developed, undertaken, reviewed, reported, and communicated in a way that is transparent, fair, full, and unbiased. The five verbs matter: honesty is not confined to the moment of publication.

  • Developing — proposals and protocols describe what will actually be done, and declare relevant interests.
  • Undertaking — the work follows the protocol; deviations are recorded rather than quietly absorbed.
  • Reviewing — assessment of others' work is impartial and free from undeclared conflicts.
  • Reporting — results are presented in full, including those that do not support the hypothesis.
  • Communicating — findings are conveyed to non-specialist audiences without overstatement.

The four adverbs are equally deliberate. Full rules out selective reporting even when every reported item is individually accurate; unbiased rules out framing that technically avoids falsehood while leaving a misleading impression.

Three concentric circles expand outward from Colleagues and Research Participants at the centre, through Society and Cultural Heritage, to Ecosystems and the Environment, with arrows marking an expanding responsibility radius and impact zone.

params.text:
An Expanding Radius of Responsibility

Respect has the widest scope of the four principles. The Code extends it well beyond the people enrolled in a study, through three widening circles of responsibility.

panels.title: Inner circle — colleagues and research participants

params.text: Participants are owed informed consent, privacy, welfare, and particular care where they are vulnerable. Colleagues are owed fair treatment, appropriate credit, and a working environment free from harassment and exploitation. Both obligations are frequently tested by seniority and power differences.

panels.title: Middle circle — society and cultural heritage

params.text: Research findings reach policymakers, practitioners, and the public. Respect at this level means communicating accurately and resisting overstatement. Where research touches cultural heritage — artefacts, sites, or community knowledge — it means recognising the communities to whom that heritage belongs.

panels.title: Outer circle — ecosystems and the environment

params.text: Research activity has material consequences: field research disturbs habitats, laboratory work generates waste, and computation consumes energy. The Code makes acknowledging and minimising this impact an integrity obligation rather than an optional courtesy.

params.text:
A Continuous State, Not a Final Step

Accountability runs the length of the research timeline. The slide's caption is the essential point: accountability is a continuous temporal state, not a final step. It does not begin at submission or end at acceptance.
Responsibility attaches from the outset — for the scientific validity of the question, for checking what is already known, and for the ethical defensibility of the proposed approach.
Covers the running of the project: data management, financial stewardship, adherence to protocols, and the arrangements that make the work traceable and reviewable.

Senior researchers are accountable for the standards of those they supervise. A supervisor who never examines a student's raw data has not discharged this responsibility, whatever the student's own conduct.
Extends past publication. Authors remain answerable for the record — responding to queries, correcting errors, and taking responsibility for how findings are used beyond the academy.

params.text:
Integrity Is an Institutional Responsibility

The first domain of good research practice concerns the environment in which research happens. The Code places clear obligations on institutions, not only on individual researchers: research organisations must actively cultivate a culture of integrity built on mutual respect and equity, diversity, and inclusion.

panels.title: Promote a culture of research integrity

params.text: Integrity should be an explicit, visible commitment — set out in policy, communicated at induction, and reinforced through training. Where researchers have to guess at the rules, the institution has not met this obligation.

panels.title: Ensure research freedom without undue pressure

params.text: Institutions must protect researchers' independence. Output targets and publication quotas that push researchers towards questionable practice are themselves an integrity problem, not merely a management style.

panels.title: Provide clear and transparent misconduct procedures

params.text: Every institution needs documented, accessible, and consistently applied procedures for handling allegations. Procedures that exist but cannot be found are functionally absent.

panels.title: Protect those who report in good faith

params.text: People who raise concerns must be protected from retaliation. The Code singles out early-career and short-term contract researchers, whose position makes them most exposed and least able to absorb the cost of speaking up.

Institutions must supply what good practice requires: secure data management, storage that supports reproducibility, and systems that make research traceable. Absent infrastructure is not a defence for poor practice, but it is an institutional failure.

Case Study 1: Research Environment

After six months as a novice researcher in a university laboratory, you meet a former classmate who now works at a commercial research organisation. She describes encountering a potential case of research misconduct involving intellectual property — and knowing exactly what to do, because her company makes certain every employee is fully briefed on the applicable rules. Her action prevented the misconduct.

The conversation prompts a realisation: you were never briefed on research rules or regulations when you signed your contract. Your mentor once referred in passing to the "standard rules of conduct in research", apparently assuming you knew them.

Checking your school's website, you find no explicit research integrity section. The university refers to its own code of conduct and to the European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity, and mentions both a complaints procedure and a research integrity committee — but no details of either are publicly available. Fellow novice researchers turn out to be equally uncertain whether written guidelines exist at all.

They also describe something else: pressure to generate ever more output, and insecurity tied to short-term contracts and scarce advancement opportunities. The incentives to succeed, they feel, outweigh the incentives to comply with good research practice.

Three institutional failures compound. No effective communication of rules — policies that exist but are not communicated do not shape behaviour. No accessible procedures — a complaints route no one can locate cannot be used. Incentive misalignment — when precarity and output pressure make shortcuts rational, the environment is generating the risk.

Brief every researcher on integrity rules at the point of appointment, not incidentally. Publish the complaints procedure and the committee's remit where researchers can find them. Examine whether assessment and contract structures are creating pressure that undermines the standards being asked for.

panels.title: What can the individual researcher do?

params.text: Ask directly for the institution's research integrity guidance — the request itself is legitimate and useful. Consult the European Code where local guidance is silent. Raise the gap collectively rather than individually, since a shared concern is harder to dismiss and safer to voice.

params.text:
Why Supervision Is an Integrity Issue

Training, supervision, and mentoring form the second practice domain. The Code's requirement is concise but demanding: senior researchers should lead by example, ensuring that those they supervise receive proper training in research integrity and that supervision is genuine rather than nominal.

Supervision failures rarely announce themselves as integrity breaches. They appear as absence — an unavailable supervisor, results dismissed without discussion, authorship decided elsewhere. The consequences are nonetheless integrity consequences.

Supervisors set the norms of a group through their own conduct far more than through stated policy. A supervisor who never inspects raw data, or who tolerates courtesy authorship, teaches that these things are acceptable.
Research integrity training is a supervisory responsibility, not solely an institutional one. Junior researchers need to know the standards before they are exposed to situations that test them.

Supervision means being available, engaging with the work, and giving feedback that lets a junior researcher progress. Prolonged absence is a supervisory failure with direct effects on both wellbeing and research quality.

The Code connects the research environment to mental health explicitly. Unsustainable working patterns are a supervisory concern, both for their own sake and because exhausted researchers make poorer judgements.

Case Study 2: Training, Supervision, and Mentoring

Lane is a second-year doctoral student working on gene expression in hepatic tumours. Her work–life balance has collapsed: weekends in the laboratory, evenings on data management and background reading, hobbies abandoned, friends unseen for weeks. Her wellbeing is suffering.

Her laboratory is among the best in the field, which also makes its climate highly competitive. Senior researchers are not always willing to help. On several occasions Lane has seen unfamiliar authors' names appear on papers at the submission stage.

Her supervisor, Prof. Smith, is known for breakthrough work in cell signalling and is aiming for Science and Nature as he works towards tenure within five years. He has so far dismissed Lane's results as too insignificant and wants her to keep going until the findings are more impressive — which may mean she does not finish her PhD on time.

Lane believes she already has enough data for a smaller journal, which would suffice for her thesis. She is uncomfortable leaving the results unpublished: the laboratory is publicly funded, so she feels the public is entitled to the findings, and another group may publish similar work first and render her effort unpublishable. Meanwhile Prof. Smith has not visited the laboratory in three months and answers emails briefly if at all.

Prof. Smith has obligations Lane cannot discharge for him: to be present and engaged, to assess results on scientific merit rather than journal prestige, to ensure Lane can complete within a reasonable timeframe, and to prevent undeserved authorship appearing on the group's papers.

panels.title: Reference: the EU Code on training, supervision, and mentoring

params.text: The Code requires senior researchers to lead by example and to provide proper supervision and mentoring. Three months of absence, and dismissal of valid results in pursuit of a more impressive outcome, both fall short of that standard.

panels.title: Mental health and poor mentoring practices

params.text: Lane's situation is a wellbeing issue as well as a supervisory one. The competitive climate, absent supervision, and open-ended timeline together produce exactly the conditions the Code asks institutions to prevent.

Two further integrity issues sit inside the case. Withholding valid publicly-funded results in the hope of a more impressive outcome contributes to publication bias. Unfamiliar names appearing at submission indicates authorship not based on contribution — a breach in its own right.

params.text:
Procedures That Protect the Result

The third practice domain covers how research is planned and carried out. Most of its requirements exist to prevent a specific failure mode: analytic decisions made after seeing the data, and then presented as though they had been made before.

panels.title: Plan according to the latest available knowledge

params.text: Research must build on what is already established. Studies that duplicate settled questions or ignore prior findings produce research waste — consuming funding, time, and participant goodwill without adding knowledge.

Protocols must consider the diversity of the populations they aim to describe. Findings drawn from narrow samples may not generalise, which limits both their scientific value and their fair application.
Funds must be used for their stated purpose and managed according to funder and institutional requirements.
Use of artificial intelligence and automated tools must comply with the standards and norms of the discipline, and must be disclosed. Accuracy of output does not remove the disclosure obligation.

Hypotheses should be formulated before analysis, and analytic plans specified in advance. Where analysis departs from the plan, the departure must be reported as such — this is what separates legitimate exploratory work from HARKing.

Two Named Failure Modes

HARKing — Hypothesizing After the Results are Known — means formulating a hypothesis once the data have been seen, then presenting it as though it had been specified in advance. The reported finding appears confirmatory when it is in fact exploratory. Because a hypothesis constructed to fit the data will always fit the data, HARKing converts a genuine test into a guaranteed success.

Spin is the related presentational failure: the linguistic or statistical inflation of results to manufacture significance the data do not support. It typically accompanies under-reporting of a study's limitations.

Case Study 3: Research Procedures

Professor Gallagher leads a psychology project on moral intuitions, working with Dr. Jones, a philosopher, and Mr. Singh, a doctoral student. Despite limited experience in the matter, Dr. Jones is named principal investigator for study design and analysis across two experiments, while Mr. Singh prepares materials and runs the experiments.

First study. Mr. Singh sends the results to Dr. Jones for analysis. Some time later, eager to include the findings in his thesis, he asks about them. Dr. Jones admits she forgot to formulate the hypothesis before analysing the data — meaning the results could be read as confirmatory whichever direction they ran. Together they decide to formulate a hypothesis that yields a positive finding. They present the results to Prof. Gallagher, who is satisfied and begins writing the paper.

Second study. Dr. Jones formulates multiple hypotheses in advance. Mr. Singh runs the study and sends the results. Dr. Jones analyses them looking only for significant differences between groups and, to reach significance, excludes participants over 60 from the analysis. She discloses this to Prof. Gallagher, who is again satisfied and proceeds with the paper, while Mr. Singh enters the results in his dissertation.

Before Mr. Singh's public defence, an internal reviewer notices that data were excluded from the second study and that only significant results were reported. At an examination board meeting, Mr. Singh admits the exclusion — and that in the first study the hypothesis was formulated after the results were known.

panels.title: Why is HARKing a problem here?

params.text: Dr. Jones's admission is the pivotal moment: with no hypothesis specified in advance, the results could be presented as confirmatory in either direction. Constructing a hypothesis to produce a positive finding converts an exploratory result into a false claim of prediction — and readers cannot detect the substitution from the published paper.

panels.title: Why is the exclusion of participants over 60 a problem?

params.text: The exclusion was not pre-specified and had no stated scientific rationale — its purpose was to reach significance. This is selective exclusion: a decision driven by the desired result rather than by the research question.

All three. Dr. Jones performed the analyses and made both decisions. Mr. Singh participated in the first and used the results in his dissertation. Prof. Gallagher, as project leader, was told about the exclusion and proceeded regardless — accountability for training and supervision does not transfer downward.

The first study should have been reported honestly as exploratory. The second should have reported the full analysis including participants over 60, with any exclusion pre-specified and justified. Prof. Gallagher should have halted the paper when the exclusion was disclosed.

params.text:
Approval Is a Starting Point, Not a Conclusion

The safeguards domain covers the protections owed to participants, collaborators, communities, and the environment. Its central requirement is that risks and harms be recognised and weighed before research begins — and, critically, monitored as the research proceeds.

Ethical approval marks the point at which a study may begin. It does not certify that every subsequent decision is sound. Protocols change, data move, and unanticipated findings surface; each of these can introduce risks the original approval never considered.

panels.title: Recognise and weigh risks and harms

params.text: Risks to participants, communities, collaborators, and the environment must be identified explicitly and weighed against anticipated benefits — before the work starts, and again whenever the protocol changes.

panels.title: Protect participants under legal and ethical provisions

params.text: Research must comply with the legal frameworks that protect participants, GDPR foremost among them in the European context. Compliance is assessed against actual data flows, not against the intention at design time.

panels.title: Apply the highest standards to boundary-spanning research

params.text: Citizen science and research crossing professional boundaries require rigorous oversight, training, and safeguards. Involving non-professional participants raises the bar for supervision rather than lowering it.

Where personal data are collected, protection depends on rigorous anonymisation or pseudonymisation protocols. Aggregate data can still identify individuals when the group is small or the categories are distinctive.

Case Study 4: Safeguards

A large study across nine European countries evaluates the structure and environment of secondary schools alongside student mental health, using a screening tool. Each research group obtained ethical approval, and the research plan was deemed GDPR compliant.

During the study, the researchers decide to share aggregate school-level data with individual schools, and also to share data from neighbouring schools. They obtain ethical approval for this protocol change. However, data sharing carries a cost and the funders decline to provide additional money. Some sites have already shared their data; in the end some schools receive the data and others do not.

Several consequences follow. Leadership at some schools, dissatisfied with the results, complain about potential bias in the research. Schools with a high proportion of a particular ethnic minority performed poorly on the assessment — and these schools receive substantially lower funding. And the mental health screening identifies some students with significant problems potentially requiring medical treatment.

panels.title: Was sharing the school-level results good practice?

params.text: Returning findings to participating schools is defensible in principle. Sharing neighbouring schools' data is harder to justify: it enables comparison and ranking that the schools did not consent to, and creates reputational risk with no clear benefit to them.

panels.title: Was ethics approval needed for the protocol change?

params.text: Yes — and the team correctly sought it. A change to the dissemination policy alters the risk profile for participants and institutions, so it requires review. Institutional research offices and the original approving committee are where that requirement is documented.

panels.title: Is it acceptable that some schools received data and others did not?

params.text: No. Unequal return of results treats participating institutions inequitably and compounds any disadvantage among those left out. Having begun, the team should have sought alternative means to complete distribution — reduced-cost formats, phased release, or institutional support — rather than stopping partway.

Complaints about research bias fall to the institutions' research integrity bodies and, where multiple countries are involved, to an agreed coordinating mechanism. This is precisely the kind of arrangement that should be settled at the start of a multi-country collaboration.

panels.title: What about the students identified as needing treatment?

params.text: This is the most serious safeguard question in the case. Screening that may detect treatable conditions creates a duty of care: the protocol should have specified in advance how findings would be communicated, to whom, and with what consent from students or parents. Discovering the issue after results are in is already too late.

That poorly-performing schools with high minority populations received lower funding illustrates how research findings can cause real harm to communities. Weighing this possibility is part of the risk assessment the safeguards domain requires.

metadata.title: Data Architecture and the FAIR Principles
metadata.extraTitle: Data Architecture and the FAIR Principles

params.text:
Data as a Research Output in Its Own Right

The fifth domain concerns how research data are collected, stored, described, and shared. Its foundation is the FAIR principles, and its governing balance is captured in a single phrase: data should be as open as possible and as closed as necessary.
Data and metadata must be locatable by both people and machines. In practice this means persistent identifiers such as DOIs, rich metadata, and deposit in indexed repositories.

Once located, data should be retrievable through open, standardised protocols. Accessible does not mean unrestricted: access may be controlled for legitimate reasons, but the conditions must be stated clearly and remain available even when the data themselves are not.
Data should use shared formats, vocabularies, and standards so they can be combined with other datasets. Proprietary formats that tie data to particular software undermine this.
Data must be described well enough that others can use them for new purposes — which requires provenance information, clear documentation, and an explicit licence.

params.text:
Openness, Protection, and Recognition

As open as possible, as closed as necessary. Openness is the default because shared data increase the return on research investment. Restriction is legitimate where privacy, confidentiality, or genuine commercial considerations require it — but restriction must be justified, not assumed.

Data are citable research products. The Code recognises datasets, metadata, protocols, code, and software as legitimate and citable outputs. They are not preparatory materials subordinate to a paper; they are results that deserve recognition in their own right.

Retention. Research data and materials must be preserved for a reasonable and clearly stated period, so that findings remain traceable and verifiable after publication.

Case Study 5: Data Practices and Management

Professor Brown, an epidemiologist, has won a prestigious grant to study how environmental, genetic, and clinical factors affect obesity prevalence in urbanised areas. The interdisciplinary team spans senior researchers, postdoctoral researchers, and doctoral students. The methodology draws on public databases (Geographic Information System and Google Street View), hospital records, genetic samples held in a hospital biobank, surveys, and participant interviews.

The sharing dispute. Working on the GIS and Street View component, one team member insists the datasets be deposited in a public repository, since the grant agreement requires FAIR principles. Others disagree. Some emphasise GDPR requirements and intellectual property rights in the collected data. Others argue data should be released only after the manuscript is published, so that nobody can pre-empt their publication plans.

The hospital records. For this component the team retrospectively collected laboratory data, histological results, and personal data of individual patients — age, sex, residential area, and occupation. They did so without ethics committee approval, assuming approval was unnecessary for records created a decade earlier. Informed consent was not obtained from the patients.

panels.title: Does FAIR require immediate public deposit?

params.text: No. FAIR is not a mandate to publish everything immediately. Accessible explicitly allows controlled access where justified. The correct approach is to deposit with clear metadata and appropriate access conditions — satisfying FAIR without disregarding GDPR or IP obligations.

panels.title: Is delaying release until publication legitimate?

params.text: A defined embargo is a recognised and acceptable practice. What is not acceptable is indefinite withholding, or treating competitive advantage as sufficient reason to keep publicly funded data closed permanently. The embargo should be stated, time-limited, and recorded in the data management plan.

panels.title: Were the hospital records handled correctly?

params.text: No. This is the clearest breach in the case. The age of the records does not remove the need for ethical review, and the data collected — age, sex, residential area, occupation, alongside laboratory and histological results — are personal data under GDPR. Retrospective research on identifiable patient records requires ethics approval and an appropriate legal basis, whether consent or a documented exemption.

panels.title: What should the team do now?

params.text: Halt processing of the hospital records, seek retrospective ethics review, and establish a lawful basis before continuing. Agree a written data management plan covering deposit, access conditions, embargo periods, and IP — the absence of which is what allowed the dispute to arise.

params.text:
Agreements Before Work, Not After Disputes

The sixth domain addresses research conducted across institutions, countries, and disciplines. Its central requirement is timing: partners must agree the terms of the collaboration at the outset, because the questions that seem premature at the start are exactly the ones that become intractable later.

panels.title: Agree goals, outputs, and standards at the beginning

params.text: All partners should agree the research goals, expected outputs, and the integrity standards that will govern the work before it starts. Where institutional policies differ between partners, the differences need to be identified and reconciled rather than discovered mid-project.

panels.title: Settle data ownership and intellectual property

params.text: Who owns the data, the samples, and any resulting IP should be documented in advance — particularly where the work may have commercial application, and particularly where partners sit in different legal jurisdictions.
Authorship expectations should be set at the start and revisited as contributions develop. Deferring the conversation until submission is when authorship disputes are made, not avoided.

All partners are responsible for the integrity of the collaboration's results. Responsibility does not concentrate in the coordinating institution, nor can partners deflect it towards whoever holds the grant.

Case Study 6: Collaborative Working

At a scientific conference, two researchers from different research backgrounds take an interest in the topic you are working on. Discussing it further during a break, you begin to see the benefits of working together. All three of you live in different countries and are at different career stages — you have just completed your doctorate, while the other two are more experienced in their fields.

The three of you draft and submit a grant proposal. You are not sure how to proceed from here.

panels.title: 1. Who should submit the proposal, and through which university?

params.text: Usually the institution of the coordinating partner, determined by the funder's eligibility rules rather than by seniority. The decision carries consequences for financial administration, liability, and IP, so it should be made deliberately and recorded — not settled by whoever has the most senior title.

panels.title: 2. Do all three need ethics approval?

params.text: Generally yes. Ethics approval is typically institution-specific, so each partner will need approval from their own committee. Requirements differ between countries, and the strictest applicable standard should govern the shared protocol.

panels.title: 3. What happens if the work has practical or commercial applications?

params.text: This must be settled in a written agreement before the work begins. IP ownership, licensing, revenue sharing, and publication rights all differ across national law and institutional policy. As the most junior partner, you are the most exposed if these terms are left informal.

panels.title: 4. How should you go about answering these questions?

params.text: Consult each institution's research office and technology transfer function. Most institutions have template consortium agreements. The European Code's guidance on collaborative working provides the integrity framework; the legal detail comes from the institutions.

panels.title: 5. What other questions should be asked?

params.text: Author order and authorship criteria. Data ownership, storage, and retention. Which partner speaks publicly about results. What happens if a partner leaves or the collaboration ends early. How disputes and any allegation of misconduct will be handled — and under whose procedures.

metadata.title: Publication, Authorship, and the Research Record
metadata.extraTitle: Publication, Authorship, and the Research Record

params.text:
Reporting the Whole Record

The seventh domain governs how results reach the scientific community and the public. Two obligations dominate: report all results, and attribute them to those who actually did the work.

Results that fail to confirm a hypothesis carry real scientific value. Suppressing them produces publication bias — a literature systematically skewed towards positive findings, which distorts every subsequent review and meta-analysis drawn from it.
Assumptions and limitations must be stated so that the robustness of the evidence is not overstated. Under-reporting limitations is the condition in which spin takes hold.

panels.title: Apply the same standards regardless of venue

params.text: The same criteria for integrity and honesty apply whether publishing in a subscription journal, an open access journal, or a preprint repository. Adjusting standards to the venue conflicts directly with the honesty principle.
Funding sources, advisory roles, commercial interests, and any relationship that could appear to compromise objectivity must be declared.

Authorship requires substantive contribution to the research, participation in drafting or critical revision, approval of the final version, and willingness to be accountable for the content. Position, funding, or facility ownership do not by themselves qualify anyone.

Case Study 7: Publication, Dissemination, and Authorship

After graduating in biomedicine you take a temporary position as a laboratory technician in the Department of Physiology, while continuing to pursue doctoral options. Interviews are unsuccessful: they want a candidate with a research publication.

In your laboratory you perform animal experiments and other experimental work, while doctoral students and postdocs handle data analysis and interpretation for publication. For one project, however, you are asked to perform the data analysis yourself, because you have experience with that method. Your results are included in a manuscript intended for a high-impact journal.

You ask the Head of Department — also the principal investigator — whether you will be a co-author. He replies that you were employed as a technician rather than a doctoral student, and that your role was technical support, not analysis. When you point out that you meet the ICMJE authorship criteria, he reminds you that the position was created specifically for you while the institution waits for a doctoral studentship, and that authorship can be discussed once you become a doctoral student.

From colleagues you learn this is not the first time. One mentions an occasion when the Head added a colleague of his as an author without the other authors knowing that person had been involved at all.

On the facts given, yes. You performed the data analysis included in the manuscript — a substantive intellectual contribution. Provided you also contribute to drafting or revision, approve the final version, and accept accountability, the criteria are met. Job title is not among them.

panels.title: What is wrong with the Head's reasoning?

params.text: It substitutes employment category for contribution. Authorship follows what a person did, not the contract they did it under. The offer to discuss authorship 'once you become a doctoral student' also makes credit conditional on future status — which is coercive, given his influence over that status.

Adding an author unknown to the other authors is gift authorship. It misrepresents who did the work and attaches accountability to someone who cannot genuinely accept it. That it has happened before indicates a pattern rather than an oversight.

Raise the matter first with the corresponding author or journal editor, citing the ICMJE criteria. If unresolved, the institution's research integrity committee or research ombudsperson is the appropriate route. The power imbalance here is real and worth acknowledging — which is exactly why the Code places a protection obligation on institutions.

panels.title: The wider question the case poses

params.text: The case asks whether you follow colleagues' example and let authorship go in order to protect your prospects. Doing so participates in the practice and helps normalise it. This is precisely the environmental pressure Case Study 1 describes — and the reason integrity is treated as a systemic responsibility rather than an individual test of character.

metadata.title: Peer Review Failures and Their Compounding Effect
metadata.extraTitle: Peer Review Failures and Their Compounding Effect

params.text:
A System Built on Trust

The final practice domain covers peer review and research assessment. Peer review grants reviewers privileged access to unpublished ideas, methods, and data. That access is granted on trust, and the obligations attached to it are correspondingly strict.

panels.title: Declare conflicts of interest and decline where they exist

params.text: A reviewer working on a competing manuscript has a disqualifying conflict. The correct response is to decline the invitation — before reading further, since the conflict exists independently of how scrupulously the review is then conducted.

panels.title: Maintain confidentiality and respect intellectual property

params.text: Manuscripts under review are confidential. They may not be shared, discussed outside the review process, or used to inform the reviewer's own work. The authors' intellectual property remains theirs until publication.

Involving a student in a review can be legitimate training — but only with the journal's knowledge and consent, and with the supervisor reading the manuscript and taking responsibility for the review submitted.
Requiring authors to cite the reviewer's own work as a condition of acceptance is an abuse of the reviewer's position, and inflates citation metrics through pressure rather than merit.

Evaluation for funding, hiring, and promotion should be transparent and justifiable, and should weigh quality, knowledge advancement, and impact rather than relying on publication counts and journal prestige.

Case Study 8: Reviewing and Assessment

Professor Daniels is a well-known sociologist whose group is working on an interdisciplinary project investigating innovative empirical methods that use social media platforms for data collection. With her team of master's and doctoral students she plans to submit a paper on the topic.

She receives an invitation to review a manuscript for an academic journal. The abstract shows significant overlap with her own group's draft. She accepts the invitation.

Short of time, she asks a doctoral student to read the manuscript and write the review. When it is ready she forwards it to the journal without reading it. The review is highly critical, recommends major revisions, and includes a request for additional citation of Prof. Daniels's own work.

Soon afterwards, Prof. Daniels and her team submit their paper to a prestigious journal. It receives extremely positive reviews and is accepted outright, published online four weeks after submission.

Weeks later the editor receives a complaint from the corresponding author of the manuscript Daniels reviewed, alleging that her published article contains one of the innovative methodological models developed by their group and described in their manuscript — and that a table in her article presents the main features of that model. They request an urgent investigation into the peer review process. Two weeks pass with no adequate response from the editorial office.

Accepting a review of work that overlaps with her group's unsubmitted manuscript was the first breach, and it precedes everything else. The correct action was to decline immediately on reading the abstract. Every later failure follows from this one.

panels.title: Failure 2 — unauthorised delegation and breach of confidentiality

params.text: Passing a confidential manuscript to a doctoral student without the journal's knowledge breaches confidentiality and exposes the student to a situation they are not positioned to refuse. Submitting the review unread compounds it — she took responsibility for an assessment she had not made.
Requiring citation of her own work as part of the revision demand uses reviewer authority for personal benefit and inflates her metrics through coercion rather than merit.

The most serious allegation is that her published paper reproduces a methodological model from the manuscript she reviewed. If substantiated, this is the appropriation of confidential intellectual property — the gravest breach available to a reviewer. The critical review that delayed the original manuscript, followed by her own rapid publication, is what makes the sequence so damaging.

The journal's silence is itself a breach. Editors are responsible for the integrity of the published record and must investigate credible allegations promptly. Two weeks without an adequate response is not a neutral delay — it disadvantages the complainants further.

The editor should open a formal investigation under COPE guidance, involving both journals and both institutions. Depending on findings, outcomes range from correction to retraction, alongside an institutional misconduct process. The doctoral student's position should be handled carefully — they were placed in this situation by a supervisor.

params.alt: Case Study 8: Reflection slide. Discussion and best practice points: Conflict of Interest — reviewing competing work; Unauthorized Delegation — giving confidential manuscripts to students; Coercive Citation — demanding self-references.

Terminology Practice

Forty-five terms from across the module, grouped into three sets. Click a card to reveal the definition, and use the shuffle control to vary the order. Working through all three sets is good preparation for the Final Assessment.

params.title: Set 1 — Principles and Framework (15 cards)

dialogs.answer: The attitude and habit of conducting research according to appropriate ethical, legal, and professional frameworks.
The application of ethical principles to fields such as study design, treatment of participants, and prevention of misuse of results.
Ensuring the quality of research through its design, methodology, analysis, and use of resources.
Developing, undertaking, reviewing, reporting, and communicating research in a transparent, fair, full, and unbiased way.
Regard for colleagues, research participants, society, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and the environment.
Responsibility for research from idea generation to publication, including its management, training and mentoring, and wider societal impact.
Internal attitude and habit, combined with external frameworks and standards, produces trustworthy research.
Five levels of engagement with research integrity: understand, apply, solve, promote, and foster.

dialogs.text: European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity
dialogs.answer: The ALLEA-published reference document for research integrity in Europe, revised in 2023 and integrated into EU research frameworks.
All European Academies — the federation of European academies of sciences and humanities that publishes the European Code of Conduct.
Bridging the Gap: Research Ethics Training and Education — the Erasmus+ project (2023-1-EL01-KA220-HED-000167028) that produced this module.
The institutional obligation to allow researchers to work independently, without undue pressure that would compromise their standards.
An institutional environment built on mutual respect and on equity, diversity, and inclusion, in which good practice is expected and supported.
The obligation to protect those who report suspected misconduct in good faith, with particular attention to early-career and short-term researchers.

dialogs.answer: The loss of value that occurs when research is poorly planned, insufficiently transparent, or duplicates knowledge already established.
Hypothesizing After the Results are Known — presenting a hypothesis formed after seeing the data as though it had been specified in advance.
Linguistic or statistical inflation of results to manufacture significance the data do not support.

dialogs.answer: The data access principle: openness is the default, with restriction permitted only where legitimately justified.
Data, metadata, protocols, code, and software recognised as legitimate research outputs deserving citation in their own right.
The requirement to preserve research data and materials for a reasonable and clearly stated period so findings remain verifiable.

params.text:
What This Module Covered

You began with the distinction between research integrity and research ethics, and with the integrity equation: internal attitude and habit combined with external frameworks produce trustworthy research. You then worked through the four principles of the European Code, the eight domains of good research practice, and a case study for each domain.

Reliability — quality across design, methodology, analysis, and resources. Honesty — transparent, fair, full, and unbiased conduct at every stage. Respect — for colleagues, participants, society, cultural heritage, and the environment. Accountability — continuous, from idea generation through to societal impact.

Research environment; training, supervision and mentoring; research procedures; safeguards; data practices and management; collaborative working; publication, dissemination and authorship; and reviewing and assessment. Each was paired with a case study showing how the requirement behaves under real conditions.

Several patterns appeared repeatedly across the cases: HARKing and selective exclusion in analysis; gift and ghost authorship; conflicts of interest left undeclared; and suppression of valid findings in pursuit of more impressive ones.

Perhaps the most important pattern is that most cases involved a structural component. Precarious contracts, output pressure, absent supervision, and assessment based on quantity rather than quality all shaped the decisions individuals made. Integrity failures are rarely purely individual.

Three Things Worth Carrying Forward

  1. Decide before you look. Hypotheses, analysis plans, exclusion criteria, and authorship should be settled before the data or the manuscript can influence the decision. Almost every analytic failure in these cases traces back to a decision made after seeing the result.
  2. Approval is a beginning, not a discharge. Ethics approval, GDPR sign-off, and institutional policy set a floor. Risks change as research proceeds, and the obligation to reassess travels with the project.
  3. Environment shapes conduct. Where good practice is costly and shortcuts are rewarded, individual resolve will not hold indefinitely. Improving conditions is part of the work — the top of the cognitive staircase.

Where to Go Next

The European Code of Conduct for Research Integrity is short and worth reading in full — Chapter 23 links to it directly. If you are working on institutional policy rather than personal practice, the SOPs4RI Toolbox and the Bonn PRINTEGER Statement are the natural next step. And if a situation in your own work resembled one of these cases more closely than was comfortable, your institution's research integrity officer exists precisely for that conversation.
